passage:
Subject: Project plan, first update

Dear Irfan Sir,

Our team of four met on Saturday and cut the project into four parts: data collection, the model, the interface and the report. Each part became a set of small cards on one online board, and every card carries a name and a date. I took the interface, Meena took the data, and the other two took the model and the report. We agreed to look at the board together for ten minutes every Tuesday and Friday. After two weeks, nine of fourteen cards have moved to done, and two late cards were noticed early. Could we show you the board on Friday?

Regards,
Nazia

qa.q: How many cards had moved to done after two weeks?
qa.a: Nine of fourteen cards have moved to done.

qa.q: What is Nazia feeling as the update is written?
qa.a: Nazia seems proud and hopeful: the progress is reported with numbers, and asking to show the board suggests confidence.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the team use if cards keep slipping, and why?
qa.a: They could hold a short root-cause talk about the slipping cards, because a board shows what is late but not why it is late.

qa.q: How might Irfan Sir see this update?
qa.a: Irfan Sir gets a clear picture of who is doing what and when, so he can judge progress quickly and offer help early.

grounding: Shows a team breaking a project into parts, giving each card an owner and a date, and checking progress briefly twice weekly.

subtype: Approach: task decomposition with a shared board [Action]
passage: Saurabh, you asked how our final-year team didn't fall apart. I'm Raghav, so you'll get the honest version. Four of us, one crop-disease detection app, eight months. In the first week we broke the project into modules: image collection, the model, the app screens, and the report. Then we broke each module into tasks small enough to finish in under a week and put them on a shared online board. Every task had one owner's name and a date. Not "the team". One name. Every Monday and Thursday at 5, we met for fifteen minutes, standing, in the lab corridor. Each person said what they'd finished, what was next, and what was blocking them. That's it. When Pooja's image collection slipped by a week, we saw it on a Thursday, not in March. Honestly, the board did half the managing for us.

qa.q: When did the team meet each week?
qa.a: Every Monday and Thursday at 5, for fifteen minutes.

qa.q: How does Raghav feel about the board?
qa.a: Raghav sounds proud and relieved, crediting the board with doing half the managing.

qa.q: What else could Saurabh's team add to this system?
qa.a: They could list risks on the board too, so problems like slipping data collection are flagged before they happen.

qa.q: How was Pooja affected by the twice-weekly reviews?
qa.a: Pooja's delay was spotted early, so the team could help while there was still time, rather than it becoming a crisis later.

grounding: Shows a team of four splitting the project into modules, putting tasks with owners and dates on a shared board, and reviewing it briefly twice a week.

subtype: Approach: task decomposition with a shared board [Action]
passage: Our team sat at the next table in the project lab, so I watched Jatin and Kavitha's group get organised while we argued. On day one, Kavitha drew four columns on the whiteboard: To do, Doing, Review, Done. Jatin broke their traffic-signal project into modules: camera input, vehicle counting, signal logic, dashboard. Each module was split into small tasks on sticky notes, each with one name and a date. Later they moved it all to an online board. Every Tuesday and Friday, the four of them stood around a laptop for ten minutes and went through it. Once I heard Jatin say, "The counting is stuck because I'm waiting for Kavitha's camera code." Kavitha moved her card to the top. I don't know whether they ever fought in private. But by December their board was mostly in Done, and ours was still an argument.

qa.q: What might Jatin have felt when the counting was stuck?
qa.a: Jatin was likely frustrated at waiting but said so calmly, and probably felt relieved when Kavitha moved her card to the top.

qa.q: What else could the observer's team borrow from this?
qa.a: They could split their project into small tasks with one owner and a date each, and hold a short review twice a week.

qa.q: How does the observer see their own team compared with Jatin's?
qa.a: The observer sees Jatin's team moving steadily while their own team is still arguing, and seems a little envious.

grounding: Illustrates a team of four breaking a project into modules on a shared board with owners and dates and reviewing it twice a week.
